8955: Scripture alone — or scripture read within tradition?
8956: Where does final authority for Christian faith and practice lie: in the Bible read by each believer, in the Bible as the sole infallible rule read within the church's creedal heritage, or in scripture and tradition together as interpreted by the church's teaching office?
8957:
Every Christian tradition reveres scripture. The disagreement is about how scripture relates to the church that received, copied, canonized and interpreted it. Three broad answers are compared here. Biblicism (sometimes called 'solo scriptura' by its critics) holds that the individual believer, reading the Bible directly, needs no creed or tradition as an authority alongside it. Sola scriptura, as the sixteenth-century magisterial Reformers framed it, holds that scripture is the only infallible rule, but that it is rightly read within the church and with the help of the ecumenical creeds as subordinate, fallible standards. The Catholic and Orthodox position holds that God's revelation is handed on through both scripture and holy tradition, and that the church (in Catholic teaching, the bishops in communion with the pope; in Orthodox teaching, the conciliar mind of the church) authentically interprets it.

The questions underneath are concrete: who settled the canon; whether the New Testament itself points to oral traditions; how disagreements among Bible readers are to be resolved; and whether any church body can be preserved from error. Each view has a long pedigree and serious defenders, and each has a characteristic weakness its rivals press.
8959:
Biblicism holds that the Bible alone, read directly by ordinary believers, is sufficient for faith and practice, and that creeds, confessions and church traditions have no binding authority at all. In its classic American Restorationist form (the Stone-Campbell movement), the slogan 'no creed but the Bible' expressed the hope that if Christians dropped human formulations and returned to the plain New Testament pattern, sectarian division would end and the primitive church would be restored.

Biblicists do not usually deny that history, scholarship or teachers can help; they deny that any of these has authority to bind conscience or to settle what the Bible means. The individual reader, guided by the Spirit and using common sense, stands directly before the text. Critics, notably Keith Mathison, call this 'solo scriptura' to distinguish it from the Reformers' sola scriptura.

8972:
Biblicism flourished in the early American republic. Nathan Hatch has shown how revolutionary ideals of liberty, suspicion of clerical elites and confidence in the common person shaped popular religion: ordinary people were told they could read the Bible for themselves and should not submit to inherited authorities. Scottish Common Sense philosophy supplied an epistemology in which a plain text, read by a sincere mind, yields its meaning.

The movement produced the Churches of Christ, the Christian Churches and the Disciples of Christ, and its instincts spread widely in nondenominational evangelicalism. Ironically, the hope of unity was followed by further divisions (for example over instrumental music and missionary societies), which critics treat as a test case of the method.

9019:
The magisterial Reformers (Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, Cranmer and their heirs) taught that scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and the final court of appeal, because it alone is God's own word. They did not reject tradition as such. They received the ecumenical creeds, read the church fathers carefully, wrote confessions, and expected scripture to be read in the communion of the church under ordained teachers. Tradition, councils and confessions are real authorities, but secondary and fallible ones, always open to correction by scripture.

Keith Mathison's *The Shape of Sola Scriptura* (2001) recast this as the difference between 'Tradition 1' (a single source of revelation, scripture, interpreted within the church's rule of faith) and 'Tradition 2' (two sources, scripture plus unwritten tradition), terms he borrowed from Heiko Oberman. On this account the Reformers sought to recover the early church's Tradition 1 position against both late-medieval Tradition 2 and radical individualism.

9032:
In the late medieval church, theologians debated whether all saving truth was contained in scripture (with tradition as its interpretation) or whether some truths came through an unwritten apostolic tradition. Heiko Oberman labeled these Tradition 1 and Tradition 2. Indulgence controversies and appeals to papal authority brought the question to a head in 1517–1521. When Luther appealed to scripture over pope and council, he was pressed to say who decides what scripture means; his answer was that scripture interprets itself, clear passages illuminating obscure ones.

The Reformers fought on two fronts: against Rome's claim that the church's teaching office stands with scripture as an authority, and against Anabaptist and spiritualist radicals whom they accused of individualism and private revelation. Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican confessions all retained the Apostles', Nicene and Athanasian Creeds.
